Semantic reranking of a first-stage result set
Dependency confusion and NuGet package source mapping

questions.prompt: You scale an ASP.NET Core app with cookie authentication from one container to three behind a load balancer, keeping the default Data Protection settings. Users are logged out at random and some form posts fail the antiforgery check. What is the cause?

choices.text: The load balancer drops cookies larger than 4 KB, so the auth tickets are lost
Antiforgery tokens expire after one request, so retries on another node fail
Cookie auth only runs on a single instance, so scaling out isn't supported
Each instance has its own key ring, so it can't decrypt another one's cookies

questions.explanation: Authentication cookies, antiforgery tokens and TempData are all protected with Data Protection keys. By default each node keeps its own key ring (in a container, often only in memory), so a request that lands on another node can't decrypt what the first one wrote, and failures look intermittent. Persist the key ring to shared storage and set the same application name; routing each user to the same node is the only alternative the docs give.

sources.title: Host ASP.NET Core in a web farm
sources.claim: By default a unique key ring is stored on each web farm node, so nodes can't decrypt each other's data; authentication, antiforgery, session and TempData depend on Data Protection, and the symptoms are intermittent sign-outs and failed antiforgery checks.

sources.title: Data Protection key management and lifetime in ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: When no persistent location is available, keys aren't persisted outside the process and are lost when it shuts down; in containers, keys should be persisted to a volume or an external provider.

questions.prompt: You add Azure AI Search's semantic ranker on top of a hybrid query. A relevant document that wasn't in the hybrid results at all still doesn't show up. Why?

choices.text: The ranker only works with pure vector queries, so hybrid queries ignore it
The ranker only reorders the top 50 results; it doesn't search the index again
The ranker drops any document whose rerankerScore is below a fixed 2.0 cutoff
The ranker needs its own embedding model, and without one it falls back to BM25

questions.explanation: Semantic ranking is a second stage: it rescores the top 50 results of the first-stage BM25 or RRF ranking with Microsoft's language models. It can't rerun the query over the whole corpus, so a document the first stage missed can't appear. Fix recall in the first stage (query, chunking, hybrid weights). It works with text, hybrid and the text part of vector queries, and it has no fixed score cutoff.

sources.title: Semantic Ranking Overview - Azure AI Search
sources.claim: Semantic ranker reranks the top 50 results of an initial BM25- or RRF-ranked result set from text, vector or hybrid queries; it can't rerun the query over the entire corpus to find new results.

questions.prompt: Your solution restores packages from nuget.org and from a private Azure Artifacts feed that hosts internal `Contoso.*` packages. Explain the dependency confusion risk, and how you would configure NuGet to close it.

model_answer.summary: With several sources NuGet searches all of them, and which one a package comes from isn't deterministic, so a look-alike `Contoso.*` package on nuget.org could be restored; package source mapping pins each package pattern to the source it must come from.
key_points: By default NuGet searches every configured source, and when a package ID exists on more than one it isn't deterministic which source it downloads from, so an attacker's public package with an internal name can get restored

Add a repo-root `nuget.config` with `<clear />` and a `packageSourceMapping` that maps `Contoso.*` to the private feed and `*` to nuget.org; the most specific pattern wins, and every package, transitive ones included, must match a pattern
Mappings are skipped for packages already in the global packages folder, so give the repo its own global packages folder (and clear it) to get the full protection
Other controls: a single private feed with upstream sources, ID prefix reservation on nuget.org, and lock files

questions.explanation: Dependency confusion abuses the fact that a package ID means nothing about where the package comes from. Source mapping fixes restore, but it doesn't stop commands like `dotnet package add` or `dotnet list package --vulnerable` from sending your package IDs to every source. Hoping internal names are unique, or pinning versions alone, doesn't close the gap.

sources.title: Package Source Mapping
sources.claim: NuGet searches all configured sources and the source isn't deterministic when a package exists on several; with package source mapping every package, including transitive ones, must match a pattern, the most specific pattern wins, mappings are ignored for packages already in the global packages folder, and mapping applies only to restore, install and update.

sources.title: Best practices for a secure software supply chain
sources.claim: When using multiple public and private feeds a package can be downloaded from any of them, so to be safe from dependency confusion know which feed each package comes from: use a single feed or a private feed with upstreams, package source mapping, lock files and package ID prefix reservation.

questions.prompt: How would you configure ASP.NET Core Data Protection for an app that runs as several instances in Azure Container Apps, and what goes wrong if you don't?

model_answer.summary: Without configuration each instance has its own, possibly in-memory, key ring, so cookies and antiforgery tokens fail across instances and after restarts; persist one shared key ring, protect it at rest and give every instance the same application name.
key_points: By default keys are per instance (and in a container may live only in memory), so cookies, antiforgery tokens and TempData protected on one instance can't be read on another, and a restart loses them
Persist the key ring to shared storage, for example `PersistKeysToAzureBlobStorage`, and protect the keys at rest, for example with `ProtectKeysWithAzureKeyVault`, using a managed identity
Call `SetApplicationName` with the same value everywhere, because Data Protection otherwise isolates apps by content root path
Don't delete old keys: keys roll every 90 days by default, and retired keys are still needed to decrypt older payloads

questions.explanation: Data Protection is the encryption behind auth cookies, antiforgery and TempData, so a missing shared key ring shows up as random sign-outs and failed posts. Sticky sessions hide the problem until an instance restarts or scales in. Pointing the key ring at a custom location turns off automatic encryption at rest, so add a `ProtectKeysWith*` call.

sources.title: Configure ASP.NET Core Data Protection
sources.claim: Keys can be persisted to Azure Blob Storage and protected with Azure Key Vault using a managed identity; SetApplicationName must match across deployments because apps are isolated by content root path by default.

sources.title: Data Protection key management and lifetime in ASP.NET Core
sources.claim: Without a persistent location keys are lost when the process shuts down; containers should use a volume or external provider; overriding the key location disables automatic encryption at rest; keys have a 90-day default lifetime and retired keys still decrypt older data, so keys shouldn't be deleted.

questions.prompt: Why does Azure AI Search's semantic ranker rescore only a short list of preranked results, rather than every document in the index?

choices.text: BM25 can't rank more than 50 documents, so later ones have no score to improve on
Its language models are costly per document, so it runs on a small preranked set
It fine-tunes itself on the top results, which needs a small and fixed training set
Vector indexes never return more than 50 results, so no larger set ever exists

questions.explanation: Semantic ranking uses resource-heavy language models, so to stay within normal query latency the system trims and summarises the inputs and sends only the top 50 first-stage results. BM25 and vector search can return more than 50 (you can page further, and `k` is configurable), and nothing is fine-tuned at query time.

sources.title: Semantic Ranking Overview - Azure AI Search
sources.claim: Semantic ranking uses a lot of resources and time, so the system consolidates and reduces its inputs; only the top 50 results of the initial ranking progress to semantic ranking.

questions.prompt: Your nuget.config maps `Contoso.*` to the private feed and `*` to nuget.org. An attacker publishes `Contoso.Billing` 99.0.0 on nuget.org. What does restore do for `Contoso.Billing`?

choices.text: Takes the highest version found on either source, so the attacker's 99.0.0 wins
Fails, because the ID matches two patterns and NuGet refuses to choose between them
Uses nuget.org, because the `*` pattern always takes precedence over the prefixes
Restores it from the private feed only, since `Contoso.*` beats the `*` pattern

questions.explanation: When several patterns match a package ID, NuGet prefers the most specific one: exact IDs first, then the longest prefix, with `*` last. So `Contoso.Billing` is looked up only on the private feed, and the public 99.0.0 is never considered. Without source mapping, NuGet would search both feeds, and which one supplied the package wouldn't be deterministic.

sources.title: Package Source Mapping
sources.claim: When multiple patterns match a package ID the most specific is preferred: exact package ID patterns first, the longest prefix next, and `*` lowest.
